name: State of Tennessee

profile.address: Hales Camp, Smyrna, Rutherford County, Middle Tennessee, Tennessee
profile.reading:
The Tennessee South Data Center sits in Smyrna, in Rutherford County southeast of Nashville, and is part of the State of Tennessee's own information technology operations rather than a leased commercial property. Public project documentation from ABEC Electric, the electrical contractor engaged to build the facility's power infrastructure, describes a building of roughly 50,000 square feet with about 25,000 square feet configured as raised floor data center space, completed around 2016. That contractor record also details dual utility feeds into the site, dual 2 megawatt generators arranged in a paralleling configuration for backup power, and redundant uninterruptible power supply systems, a combination consistent with a facility built to keep running through a single utility outage or generator failure.

No Tennessee state government source has published an official critical IT load figure in megawatts for the facility, so while the generator sizing gives a sense of the backup power envelope, it does not by itself establish how much of that capacity is dedicated to running servers versus supporting cooling, lighting, and other building loads. That is a common gap in public records for government data centers. Contractors who built the electrical plant will describe what they installed, but the agency operating the finished building rarely publishes a separate operational capacity figure of its own.

One naming confusion is worth clearing up directly. There is a separate Tennessee State Data Center associated with the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, but that is the state's affiliate site in the U.S. Census Bureau's State Data Center program, a network that distributes census and demographic statistics to researchers and the public. It has nothing to do with physical server infrastructure and should not be confused with this Smyrna facility, which is real estate housing actual state government computing equipment.

Rutherford County has grown rapidly as part of the Nashville metro area over the past two decades, and Smyrna in particular has attracted industrial and logistics investment, including a major Nissan manufacturing plant nearby, which speaks to the area's utility and workforce infrastructure. Locating a state government data center there, rather than directly in Nashville, fits a broader pattern of state agencies siting sensitive infrastructure outside the densest parts of a capital region while staying close enough for staff and connectivity. Beyond the building's size, floor configuration, and backup power description from the electrical contractor's own project record, no further technical or capacity detail about the Tennessee South Data Center is publicly available.

reading:
The State of Tennessee appears in this registry through Strategic Technology Solutions, the division of the Department of Finance and Administration that acts as the state's central information technology service bureau for its departments. The division traces its origins to 1958, when the first computer was installed in the Department of Finance and Administration to run payroll, and to the early 1970s, when state computing functions were centralised into it by executive order. It staffs the Information Systems Council and runs the state's geographic information systems and vendor management offices. Its chief information officer is Kristin Darby.

The single facility in this record is the Tennessee South Data Center in Smyrna, Rutherford County, southeast of Nashville. The most specific public description of it comes not from the state but from ABEC Electric, the electrical contractor that built its power infrastructure. That project record describes a 50,000 square foot facility with 25,000 square feet of data centre space, a 2N redundant electrical distribution system, a 2N uninterruptible power supply plant, an N plus one generator plant with a paralleling switchboard, two 3,000 amp underground utility services at 277 and 480 volts, two 2,000 kilowatt backup generator services, and a SCADA monitoring system.

Those figures are not interchangeable and should not be collapsed into a single capacity number. The two 3,000 amp services are utility power, the electrical service entering the building. The two 2,000 kilowatt units are standby diesel generation, sized to carry the building through a utility outage. Neither is a critical IT load, and no Tennessee state government publication states one. The state has published no square footage of its own, no completion date and no capacity for this facility, so everything technical above rests on a contractor's project page rather than on the agency that operates the building. That is a common gap for government data centres. The firm that installed the electrical plant will describe what it installed, while the department running the finished building has no reason to publish an operating figure.

Two further cautions belong on this page. First, the Tennessee State Data Center associated with the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, is not this facility and is not a computing facility at all. It is Tennessee's affiliate in the United States Census Bureau's State Data Center programme, a network that distributes demographic statistics to researchers, and the near identical name is a persistent source of confusion in secondary sources.

Second, the OpenStreetMap object behind this row is not a building. It is a fenced industrial land use polygon, tagged landuse=industrial with barrier=fence, and the data centre name, operator and telecom tags were added to it on 21 May 2026 in changeset 182983072, a 7,531 change bulk edit whose comment describes mapping Middle Tennessee Electric rural distribution lines. The facility itself is real, but the registry's geometry is a parcel outline captured incidentally during a power grid mapping run, and a reverse geocode of its centre returns a nearby apartment complex rather than the data centre. Treat the coordinates as approximate and the stored address as a nearest match rather than a street address.
